Female bighorn sheep typically give birth to a single calf per litter [N_R_i = single calf per litter], and under favorable conditions in the wild, they may produce one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], a maximum reproductive rate observed in populations with abundant forage. Neonatal female offspring have a wet weight at birth of 4,400 grams [Wwb = 4,400 grams], a modest mass that reflects the precocial nature of these newborn animals. This initial body size allows the calf to be mobile within hours of parturition, an adaptation linked to the steep, rocky terrain the species inhabits. The reproductive strategy of producing a single, well-developed offspring contrasts with that of other caprids of similar body mass, which occasionally produce twins at a higher frequency. Female lambs progress through a suckling juvenile stage during which they depend entirely on their mother's milk, and the transition to nutritional independence occurs at weaning. The time since birth at weaning for this species is 152 days [tx = 152 days] at a core body temperature of 38.0 °C [T = 38.0 °C], a duration that aligns with the prolonged parental investment observed in mountain ungulates inhabiting resource-limited alpine environments.

The gestation time for female calves is 180 days [tg = 180 days] measured at a maternal core temperature of 38.0 °C [T = 38.0 °C], a period that reflects the significant foetal development required for a precocial newborn capable of navigating rugged slopes. Ewes in good nutritional condition prior to the rut are more likely to conceive early and sustain the pregnancy through the harsh winter months, when forage quality declines substantially. After parturition, the neonate begins nursing almost immediately, ingesting colostrum rich in immunoglobulins that provide passive immunity during the critical first weeks of life. The lactating female's energetic demands increase markedly, requiring her to seek out productive foraging patches to maintain body condition while provisioning the calf. Field records indicate that the ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 70,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 70,000 grams], though individuals can range from 34 to 91 kilograms depending on regional forage availability and population density. This adult body mass is attained gradually over several years of growth, with young ewes typically reaching skeletal maturity before accumulating substantial fat reserves necessary for successful reproduction.

Male bighorn sheep exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism, attaining an ultimate wet weight of 100,000 grams [Wwi = 100,000 grams], with documented individuals ranging from 58 up to 143 kilograms across different herds. Rams continue to add mass well beyond the onset of sexual maturity, investing heavily in horn growth and musculature that confer advantages during intrasexual combat for access to ewes during the autumn rut. At a typical core body temperature of 38.0 °C [T = 38.0 °C], the time since birth at puberty for females is 707 days [tp = 707 days], meaning that most ewes become reproductively active during their second autumn, while the time since birth at puberty for males is 749 days [tp = 749 days], a slightly delayed maturation that allows young rams to develop sufficient body size and horn development before competing for mating opportunities. This modest difference in pubertal timing between the sexes is consistent with patterns observed in other polygynous ungulates where male reproductive success depends heavily on competitive ability.

The maximum lifespan of bighorn sheep in the wild has been documented at 20.6 years [am = 20.6 years], a longevity recorded at a core body temperature of 38.0 °C [T = 38.0 °C], though most individuals succumb to predation, disease, or environmental stress well before reaching this upper limit. Old ewes sometimes survive longer than rams, which experience higher mortality rates from fighting injuries and winter mortality once their body condition declines with age. Among the factors influencing survival, pneumonia outbreaks caused by Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae have been identified as a major source of population die-offs, particularly in reintroduced herds. Senescence in this species is characterized by progressive tooth wear, which reduces foraging efficiency and leads to a gradual decline in body condition during the winter months. Comparative data from long-term studies in the Rocky Mountains indicate that individuals inhabiting lower-elevation ranges with milder winters tend to achieve greater longevity than those in high alpine environments.

The wet weight at weaning for female calves is approximately 28,000 grams [Wwx = approximately 28,000 grams], a value consistent with the rapid pre-weaning growth observed in other large-bodied mountain ungulates, reflecting both the high nutritional quality of maternal milk and the selective pressure for early independence before winter conditions deteriorate. Weaned juveniles then enter a sub-adult phase during which they associate in nursery bands with their mothers and other ewes, learning critical foraging routes and escape terrain used to evade predators such as cougars and coyotes. By their second year, young rams disperse from these maternal groups to join bachelor herds, where they begin establishing the dominance hierarchies that will shape their future reproductive success. Bighorn sheep maintain a relatively stable core temperature of 38.0 °C [T = 38.0 °C] throughout their active periods, which supports the energetic demands of locomotion across steep, rocky landscapes and thermoregulation in alpine environments where ambient temperatures fluctuate widely.
